MHHS2401 · Musculoskeletal System · Week 2 · L3

Arm, Elbow & Anterior Forearm — the flexor machinery

One lecture, built the way the limb is built: the bones that meet, the joints they make, the muscles that move them, and the injuries that follow — each structure given its own treatment, decoded from Dr Strkalj's L3 using its own figures.

Covers LO 1–6 21 plates Clinical ×5 Recall checklist

How to use this guide

Each section carries a reference code like §5.1. Every figure is a Plate from the lecture with a Label Key; the tables summarise, the prose explains. The coloured tags mark the extras:

Reasoning
The why — and how one structure sets up the next.

A trick to lock it in.

Why it matters in the clinic.
§0Part A · orientation

Orientation — how this lecture is built

Two regions, four compartments, and a deliberate order: bones → joints → muscles → what breaks.

The upper limb here splits into the arm (brachium — shoulder to elbow) and the forearm (antebrachium — elbow to wrist). In each region, deep fascia and its intermuscular septa wall the muscles into an anterior (flexor) and a posterior (extensor) compartment — four compartments in all, each served by its own nerve.

Reasoning · why bones and joints come first

You cannot explain how the biceps supinates, why the elbow dislocates backwards, or what a "pulled elbow" actually is until you know which surfaces meet and what holds them together. So this guide builds the way the limb is built — lay down the bones (§1), assemble the joints they form (§2–§3), see how those joints fail (§4), then hang the muscles that drive them (§5–§7) and the overuse injury that follows (§8). Each part is the foundation the next one stands on.

Memory hook · one rule for the whole limb

Anterior compartment = flexors; posterior compartment = extensors — in both the arm and the forearm, and the nerve follows the compartment. Get that and every muscle below has a home.

§1LO1 · bones

Bones — distal humerus, proximal radius & ulna

The three surfaces and three pockets that make the elbow work — feature by feature.

§1.1Distal humerus

As the humerus approaches the elbow its shaft flares outward as the medial and lateral supracondylar ridges — long, narrow raised bands — which end below as the epicondyles. The lateral epicondyle is the smaller; the medial epicondyle is the larger and more prominent (you can feel it on the inside of your own elbow). Between the epicondyles sits the condyle, the articular block, which carries two different surfaces.

The anterior surface carries the condyle and, above it, two pockets:

  • The capitulum — the lateral, rounded ("little head") surface — takes the head of the radius.
  • The trochlea — the medial, spool-shaped pulley — takes the trochlear notch of the ulna.
  • The radial fossa (above the capitulum) receives the head of the radius during flexion.
  • The coronoid fossa (above the trochlea) receives the coronoid process of the ulna during flexion.

The posterior surface carries one large pocket: the olecranon fossa, which receives the olecranon of the ulna during extension.

Plate 1.1 maps every one of these onto the anterior and posterior views.

Label Key
Capitulum · trochlea
Lateral rounded surface for the radius head; medial pulley for the ulnar trochlear notch.
Radial & coronoid fossae
Anterior pockets receiving the radius head & ulnar coronoid in flexion.
Olecranon fossa
Posterior pocket receiving the olecranon in extension.
Medial / lateral epicondyles
Non-articular projections (medial larger); supracondylar ridges above.
Summary — articular surfaces & fossae
FeatureSurfaceArticulates / receives
CapitulumAnterior, lateralHead of the radius
TrochleaAnterior, medialTrochlear notch of the ulna
Radial fossaAnteriorRadius head in flexion
Coronoid fossaAnteriorCoronoid process in flexion
Olecranon fossaPosteriorOlecranon in extension
Reasoning · why three fossae

The fossae are clearance pockets shaped by the arc of motion. In full flexion the radius head and the ulnar coronoid swing forward and up — so they need somewhere to go: the radial and coronoid fossae on the front. In full extension the ulnar olecranon swings back — into the olecranon fossa on the back. The bone is hollowed exactly where a moving part would otherwise collide. Form follows the movement.

Memory hook · which surface takes which bone

Capitulum is lateral and rounded → caps the radius head (also rounded). Trochlea is a pulley (Greek trochlea = pulley) → runs the ulna's trochlear notch. "Capitulum–radius, trochlea–ulna."

Clinical / real-world · the medial epicondyle is crowded

The prominent medial epicondyle is more than a bump: it is the common flexor origin (the overuse point in golfer's elbow, §8), and the ulnar nerve passes in a groove directly behind it — the "funny bone" you hit. That is why a blow, or a medial-epicondyle fracture, threatens the ulnar nerve.

§1.2Proximal radius & ulna

In the anatomical position the radius is the lateral bone of the forearm and the ulna the medial. Each carries a set of features you will meet again as joint surfaces (§2–§3) and muscle attachments (§5).

The proximal radius has three parts: the head — a disc with a concave superior surface that sits on the capitulum, and a rim that spins inside the anular ligament (§3); the neck just below it; and the radial tuberosity, a medial bump that anchors the biceps brachii.

The proximal ulna has four features: the trochlear notch, a deep C that grips the humeral trochlea (the heart of the hinge); the coronoid process, its anterior lip; the radial notch on the lateral side, which takes the radius head (the proximal radioulnar joint, §3); and the ulnar tuberosity, which anchors the brachialis. Posteriorly the ulna projects as the olecranon (triceps insertion, and the point of the elbow).

Plate 1.2 shows the head/neck/tuberosity of the radius and the notches of the ulna.

Label Key
Radius
Head (concave, on the capitulum), neck, radial tuberosity (biceps brachii).
Ulna
Trochlear notch, coronoid process, radial notch, ulnar tuberosity (brachialis); olecranon posteriorly.
Reasoning · the tuberosities predict the muscles

Two named tuberosities, two big elbow flexors: the radial tuberosity anchors the biceps (which pulls on the radius, so it can also rotate it — supination, §5), while the ulnar tuberosity anchors the brachialis (which pulls on the ulna, which can't rotate — so brachialis is a pure flexor). The bump you learn now explains the muscle's job later.

§2LO2 · joint

The elbow joint

A hinge from two surfaces, held by side ligaments, weak front and back — and how it reads on an X-ray.

The elbow is a synovial hinge joint. Its articular surfaces are exactly the §1 bones meeting: the capitulum with the head of the radius, and the trochlea with the trochlear notch of the ulna. A hinge has a single axis, so its movements are flexion and extension only (rotation of the forearm belongs to the radioulnar joints, §3 and §6).

§2.1Capsule & ligaments

A single fibrous capsule encloses the joint, lined inside by a synovial membrane. Critically, that membrane is continuous with the proximal radioulnar joint (§3) — the elbow and the proximal radioulnar joint share one synovial cavity. The capsule is deliberately uneven: weak anteriorly and posteriorly, but thickened at the sides into two collateral ligaments.

  • The radial (lateral) collateral ligament reinforces the lateral side.
  • The ulnar (medial) collateral ligament reinforces the medial side and has three bands — anterior, posterior and oblique.

Plate 2.1 shows the capsule, both collateral ligaments and the anular ligament in a dissection.

Label Key
Joint capsule
Fibrous, synovial-lined; weak anteriorly/posteriorly.
Radial & ulnar collateral ligaments
Side reinforcements resisting varus/valgus stress.
Anular ligament of radius
Rings the radius head (proximal radioulnar joint).
Common flexor / brachialis tendon
Muscle attachments crossing the joint (shown cut).
Reasoning · strong at the sides, weak front and back

A hinge must bend freely front-to-back but must not wobble side-to-side. So the capsule is reinforced exactly where side-to-side (varus/valgus) stress lands — the collateral ligaments — and left thin where it must fold open and shut during flexion/extension. That trade-off has a price: the thin anterior capsule is the weak point a dislocating force punches through (§4).

Reasoning · one capsule, two movements

Look at the surface shapes. The trochlea is a deep pulley locked into the ulnar notch → it permits only a swing in one plane (flexion/extension). The capitulum is a ball that lets the radius head spin → it permits rotation (pronation/supination). Two geometries under one shared capsule is why the elbow flexes and the forearm rotates here.

§2.2The three bony points — reading the joint

Three landmarks you can palpate — the medial epicondyle, the lateral epicondyle and the olecranon — hold a fixed relationship: they line up horizontally in extension and form an equilateral triangle in flexion.

Plate 2.2 shows this alignment in extension vs flexion on the skeleton and the living elbow.

Label Key
Three points
Medial & lateral epicondyles + olecranon.
Extension
The three points align horizontally.
Flexion
The three points form a triangle (disrupted in dislocation).
Clinical / real-world · a bedside test

Because the triangle depends on the bones being in joint, it is disrupted in a dislocation (the bones have moved relative to each other) but preserved in a supracondylar fracture (the whole distal humerus breaks, yet the three points keep their relationship). Checking the triangle is a quick way to tell a dislocated elbow from a fractured one before imaging.

§2.3The elbow on X-ray

The same features you learned as bone (§1) are what you read on a radiograph — the humerus with its supracondylar ridges and epicondyles, the trochlea/capitulum, the olecranon and coronoid, and the humeroulnar and humeroradial joint spaces.

Plate 2.3 labels the elbow radiograph feature-by-feature.

Label Key
Humerus features
Supracondylar ridges, epicondyles, trochlea, capitulum, olecranon & coronoid fossae.
Joint spaces
Humeroulnar & humeroradial joints; radial head, neck & tubercle.

§2.4Carrying angle

The carrying angle is the angle between the long axes of the arm and forearm in the anatomical position. It is greater in females, and it lets the swinging upper limbs clear the hips and keep a carried load away from the body. The lecture notes the angle disappears when the forearm is supinated.

Plate 2.4 contrasts the angle between a typical male and female.

Label Key
Carrying angle
Between the arm & forearm axes in the anatomical position; greater in females.
Function
Lets the swinging limb clear the hips / a carried load.
§3LO2 · joint

Proximal radioulnar joint

A pivot in a ring — half of the forearm's rotation.

The proximal radioulnar joint is a synovial pivot joint. Its surfaces are the head of the radius turning against the radial notch of the ulna (a notch is an indentation on the surface), and the anular ligament — a fibrous collar — wraps the radius head and holds it against the ulna. Its movements are pronation and supination. Because its synovial cavity is continuous with the elbow's (§2.1), the two work as one capsule.

Plate 3.1 shows the anular ring in transverse section and the radius pivoting within it.

Label Key
Anular ligament
Ring holding the radius head against the radial notch of the ulna.
Axis of rotation
Radius head spins in the ring → pronation/supination; ulna stays fixed.
Reasoning · rotation takes two joints, not one

Pronation/supination is the radius spinning against the ulna. That happens at both ends at once: proximally the radius head spins inside the anular ligament (here), and distally the radius swings around the ulnar head (§6). The ulna stays put; the radius rolls over it. Jam either joint and forearm rotation is lost — which is why we return to it in §6.

Memory hook · anular = a ring

Anular ligament = an annulus (ring) round the radius head. Tear its distal attachment and the head slips out of the ring — that's the "pulled elbow" in §4.

§4LO5 · clinical

Elbow injuries

Each injury is the anatomy of §2–§3 failing at its weak point.

§4.1Posterior dislocation of the elbow

A fall on the hand with the elbow flexed drives the distal humerus forward — through the weak anterior part of the fibrous capsule (§2.1) — so the ulna and radius end up behind the humerus. Because of the forces involved it commonly comes with a tear of the (ulnar) collateral ligament and a fracture of the head of the radius, the coronoid process, or the olecranon.

§4.2Pulled elbow (subluxation of the radial head)

More common in preschool children: a sudden pull on the upper limb tears the distal attachment of the anular ligament at the neck of the radius (§3), and the radial head slips partly out of the ring.

§4.3Olecranon bursitis ("student's elbow")

The subcutaneous olecranon bursa sits over the point of the elbow; repeated pressure or irritation inflames it, giving a fluctuant swelling — hence "student's elbow".

Plate 4.1 shows the inflamed olecranon bursa.

Label Key
Olecranon bursa
Subcutaneous sac over the olecranon — inflamed here.
Swelling
Fluctuant swelling at the point of the elbow.
Clinical / real-world · the anatomy predicts the injury

Read each injury back to §2–§3. Dislocation exploits the deliberately weak anterior capsule — the price of a mobile hinge — and can drag its collateral ligament and nearby bony processes with it. Pulled elbow exploits the anular ligament: a young child's radial head isn't fully formed, so a yank slips it out from under the ring. "Student's elbow" is the subcutaneous olecranon bursa, right where you rest your elbow, getting inflamed. Nothing here is random; each is a named structure giving way.

§5LO3 · muscles

Muscles of the arm

Three flexors in front, one big extensor behind — each one, and why its attachments set its job.

The brachial fascia wraps the arm; its medial and lateral intermuscular septa run in to the humerus, dividing the arm into an anterior and a posterior compartment — each with its own nerve. Both compartments act mainly on the elbow, though some muscles cross the shoulder too.

Plate 5.1 shows the arm's muscles with the nerves threading through.

Label Key
Musculocutaneous nerve
Supplies the anterior (flexor) compartment.
Median & ulnar nerves
Pass through the arm to the forearm/hand (not arm muscles).
Radial nerve
Supplies the posterior (extensor) compartment.

§5.1Anterior compartment — musculocutaneous nerve

Three muscles, all carrying brach- (arm) in their name, all supplied by the musculocutaneous nerve.

Biceps brachii has two proximal heads: the long head from the supraglenoid tubercle of the scapula and the short head from the coracoid process. The two bellies unite and the tendon crosses the elbow to insert on the radial tuberosity. A triangular sheet — the bicipital aponeurosis — peels off the tendon and fans across the cubital fossa. Because it pulls on the radius, biceps is both a flexor of the elbow and a powerful supinator of the forearm. Plate 5.2.

Label Key
Two heads
Long head (supraglenoid tubercle) + short head (coracoid process).
Insertion
Radial tuberosity (+ bicipital aponeurosis) → flexes elbow & supinates.

Brachialis lies deep to the biceps. It runs from the midshaft of the humerus to the ulnar tuberosity, and is the chief flexor of the forearm. Coracobrachialis runs from the coracoid process to the mid-shaft of the humerus — its name spelling out its attachments — and is a weak flexor and adductor of the arm. Plate 5.3.

Label Key
Brachialis
Humeral shaft → ulnar tuberosity; chief flexor of the forearm (deep to biceps).
Coracobrachialis
Coracoid process → mid-humerus; weak flexor & adductor of the arm.
Summary — anterior arm (musculocutaneous nerve)
MuscleOriginInsertionAction
Biceps brachiiLong: supraglenoid tubercle; short: coracoid processRadial tuberosity (+ bicipital aponeurosis)Flexes elbow; powerful supinator
BrachialisMidshaft of humerusUlnar tuberosityChief flexor of the forearm
CoracobrachialisCoracoid processMid-shaft of humerusWeak flexor & adductor of the arm
Reasoning · attachment → leverage → action

This is the whole point of learning the bumps in §1. The biceps inserts on the radial tuberosity; because the radius can rotate, pulling that tendon doesn't just bend the elbow — it unwinds the radius into supination (think turning a screwdriver or a right-handed screw). The brachialis inserts on the ulna, which can't rotate, so all its force goes into one job — pure flexion — making it the reliable "workhorse" flexor whatever the forearm is doing. And the triceps (below) inserts on the olecranon, a long lever sticking out behind the elbow's axis, giving it a strong extension moment. Same bones, three attachments, three different mechanical outcomes — that is leverage.

Clinical / real-world · the bicipital aponeurosis

The bicipital aponeurosis crosses the cubital fossa as a protective roof over the brachial artery and median nerve — exactly the structures under a blood-pressure cuff and the brachial pulse. It also shields them when the median cubital vein above it is used for taking blood.

§5.2Posterior compartment — radial nerve

The triceps brachii (with the small anconeus) fills the back of the arm, supplied by the radial nerve. Its three heads converge on one tendon into the olecranon: the long head from the infraglenoid tubercle of the scapula, the medial head from the posterior humerus below the radial groove, and the lateral head from the posterior humerus above the radial groove. Triceps is the chief extensor of the forearm; the long head, crossing the shoulder, also stabilises the humeral head when the arm is abducted. Plate 5.4.

Label Key
Long / medial / lateral heads
Long from infraglenoid tubercle; medial/lateral from posterior humerus (below/above the radial groove).
Insertion
Olecranon; chief extensor; long head stabilises the abducted humerus.
Memory hook · nerve by compartment

Anterior arm = flexors = MusculoCutaneous. Posterior arm = extensors = Radial. The radial nerve runs in the radial groove of the humerus — which is exactly the landmark that splits the medial and lateral heads of triceps.

§5.3Surface anatomy of the arm

On the living arm you can identify the biceps belly with its medial and lateral bicipital grooves, the biceps tendon and bicipital aponeurosis dipping into the cubital fossa, the brachialis emerging either side of the biceps, the deltoid above, and the triceps with the olecranon behind.

Plate 5.5 maps these onto anterior-oblique and posterior views.

Label Key
Anterior
Biceps belly, medial/lateral bicipital grooves, biceps tendon & bicipital aponeurosis into the cubital fossa; brachialis.
Posterior
Deltoid above; triceps & olecranon behind.
§6LO4 · bones & joint

Forearm bones & the distal radioulnar joint

The membrane that binds two bones, and the second pivot that finishes rotation.

The forearm is the region between the elbow and the wrist. Its two bones, the radius (lateral) and ulna (medial), are tied together along their shafts by the interosseous membrane.

The interosseous membrane is a sheet of fibrous tissue that does three jobs: it stabilises the two bones against each other, it provides an attachment surface for deep forearm muscles, and its gaps let blood vessels pass between the front and back of the forearm. Together with the intermuscular septum of the antebrachial (deep) fascia it also divides the forearm into two compartments — an anterior (flexor/pronator) and a posterior (extensor/supinator).

Plate 6.1 shows the features of the distal radius & ulna.

Label Key
Distal radius
Ulnar notch (for the ulnar head), styloid process + carpal articular surface.
Distal ulna
Head of ulna + styloid; interosseous membrane binds the shafts.

§6.1Distal radioulnar joint

The distal radioulnar joint is a synovial pivot joint: the head of the ulna against the ulnar notch of the radius. A fibrocartilaginous articular disc unites the joint and, importantly, separates it from the cavity of the wrist joint. Anterior and posterior ligaments — thickenings of the joint capsule — strengthen it. Its movements are pronation and supination.

§6.2Pronation & supination

Rotating the forearm is a two-joint act. In supination the radius and ulna lie parallel (palm up); in pronation the radius crosses over the ulna (palm down). The muscles that drive it are the supinators (biceps brachii, supinator) against the pronators (pronator teres, pronator quadratus, §7).

Plate 6.2 shows the radius crossing the ulna between supination and pronation.

Label Key
Supination
Radius & ulna parallel (palm up); biceps & supinator.
Pronation
Radius crosses over the ulna (palm down); pronator teres & pronator quadratus.
Reasoning · the two pivots work as one

Forearm rotation happens at both radioulnar joints together: proximally the radius head spins in the anular ring (§3), distally the radius swings around the ulnar head (here). The ulna stays fixed and the radius rolls over it, while the interosseous membrane stays taut to keep the bones together and pass load between them. That's why an injury jamming either radioulnar joint — or a badly-set forearm fracture — costs you pronation/supination even if the elbow hinge is fine.

Clinical / real-world · a load-sharing strap

Most force enters the forearm at the wrist through the radius, but leaves at the elbow largely through the ulna. The obliquely-running fibres of the interosseous membrane are the strap that transfers that load from radius to ulna — which is why disrupting it (with a fracture) destabilises the whole forearm, not just one bone.

§6.3The two compartments in cross-section

Plate 6.3 shows the anterior and posterior compartments walled off by the interosseous membrane and the fascial septa.

Label Key
Anterior compartment
Flexors/pronators (mostly median nerve).
Posterior compartment
Extensors/supinators (radial nerve); split by the interosseous membrane & septa.
§7LO6 · muscles

Anterior compartment of the forearm

Flexors and pronators — one common origin, three layers, one nerve (nearly). Muscle by muscle.

The anterior forearm muscles are the flexors and pronators, plus extrinsic muscles of the hand. Most share a common origin on the medial epicondyle, and most are supplied by the median nerve — except 1½ muscles (flexor carpi ulnaris, and the medial half of flexor digitorum profundus) which take the ulnar nerve. They lie in four layers, grouped as superficial, intermediate and deep.

Anterior vs posterior forearm (overview)
Anterior compartmentPosterior compartment
Common attachmentMedial epicondyle of humerusLateral epicondyle of humerus
FunctionFlexors & pronators; extrinsic hand musclesExtensors & supinators; extrinsic hand muscles
InnervationMedian nerve (except 1½ by ulnar)Radial nerve
Reasoning · "remote control" hands

These are extrinsic muscles of the hand: the bulky belly sits up in the forearm and a long tendon reaches down to the fingers — a "remote control". Putting the engines in the forearm keeps the hand light and nimble enough for fine movement. The cost: many of them bundle onto a single common tendon at the medial epicondyle, which becomes the shared stress point in §8.

§7.1Superficial group (4)

All four arise from the medial epicondyle, radial-to-ulnar across the forearm:

  • Pronator teres — inserts on the mid-shaft of the radius; it pronates the forearm (and weakly flexes the elbow).
  • Flexor carpi radialis — passes obliquely to insert on the base of the 2nd metacarpal; it flexes and abducts the hand at the wrist.
  • Palmaris longus — absent in ~14% of people; it blends into the palmar aponeurosis, so it flexes the wrist and tightens the aponeurosis.
  • Flexor carpi ulnaris — inserts on the pisiform, hook of the hamate and 5th metacarpal; it flexes and adducts the hand at the wrist. It is the exception to the nerve rule — supplied by the ulnar nerve.

Plate 7.1 shows the superficial flexors fanning from the medial epicondyle.

Label Key
Common origin
Medial epicondyle → pronator teres, FCR, palmaris longus, FCU.
Actions
Wrist flexion; FCR abducts, FCU adducts; pronator teres pronates.
Memory hook · the superficial four + the odd nerve

Radial → ulnar: Pronator teres · Flexor Carpi Radialis · Palmaris Longus · Flexor Carpi Ulnaris. Everything here is median except FCU (ulnar). Note the pair of wrist movers: FCR abducts (radial side), FCU adducts (ulnar side).

§7.2Intermediate group (1)

Flexor digitorum superficialis (FDS) is the only muscle of the intermediate layer. It has a broad origin — the medial epicondyle, the coronoid process of the ulna, and the anterior border of the radius — and inserts on the middle phalanges of the medial four digits. It therefore flexes the middle phalanges at the proximal interphalangeal (PIP) joints and the proximal phalanges at the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joints. Nerve: median.

Plate 7.2 shows the two heads of FDS and the nerves/vessels passing with it.

Label Key
Two heads
Humero-ulnar head + radial head of FDS.
Relations
Median nerve & ulnar artery pass deep to it; inserts on the middle phalanges.

§7.3Deep group (3)

  • Flexor pollicis longus — from the anterior surface of the radius and the interosseous membrane to the base of the distal phalanx of the thumb; it flexes the thumb (pollex).
  • Flexor digitorum profundus (profundus = deep) — from the proximal anterior surface of the ulna to the bases of the distal phalanges of the medial four digits; it flexes the DIP and MCP joints and assists wrist flexion. Nerve: median, except its medial half which is ulnar (the "½" in the 1½ rule).
  • Pronator quadratus — a small square muscle spanning the distal anterior surfaces of the radius and ulna; it pronates the forearm.

Plate 7.3 shows the deep flexors and pronator quadratus.

Label Key
Flexor pollicis longus
Radius + interosseous membrane → distal phalanx of thumb.
Flexor digitorum profundus
Ulna → distal phalanges of medial 4 digits (medial ½ ulnar nerve).
Pronator quadratus
Distal radius↔ulna; pronates.
Reasoning · two flexors per finger, stacked

Each finger gets two long flexors, and their reach is set by where they insert: FDS stops at the middle phalanx (bending the PIP joint), while FDP runs past it to the distal phalanx (bending the DIP). Test them separately in clinic by holding the other fingers straight (isolating FDP) or holding the finger base (isolating FDS) — the anatomy is the exam manoeuvre.

Memory hook · FDS vs FDP reach & the ulnar 1½

Superficialis stops Short (middle phalanges); Profundus goes Past (distal phalanges). Ulnar nerve does "1½ muscles": all of FCU + the medial half of FDP — everything else anterior is median.

§7.4Surface anatomy of the forearm

At the wrist you can find the palmaris longus tendon (when present) and the flexor carpi radialis tendon flanking the midline, the site of the median nerve between them, the cubital fossa proximally, the styloid processes of radius and ulna, the anatomical snuff box and the course of the radial artery laterally.

Plate 7.4 maps these on the pronated and supinated forearm.

Label Key
Wrist tendons
Palmaris longus & flexor carpi radialis tendons flank the median nerve.
Landmarks
Cubital fossa, styloid processes, anatomical snuff box, radial artery course.
§8LO5 · clinical

Medial epicondylitis — golfer's elbow

The §7 common origin, failing under repetition.

Overuse of the flexor-pronator muscles microtraumatises their common tendon at the medial epicondyle. The repeated micro-injury triggers an inflammatory reaction that, over time, leads to fibrosis and calcification of the common tendon.

Medial epicondylitis at a glance
Detail
Risk activitiesRepetitive wrist flexion + forearm pronation with ball release — golf, baseball, weightlifting, bowling, tennis (forehand)
SymptomsPain around the medial epicondyle, radiating antero-inferiorly; worse with wrist/forearm movement and gripping
TreatmentMainly conservative: rest, ice, activity modification (6–12 weeks off throwing), passive stretching, NSAIDs

Plate 8.1 — the causative movement and imaging of the medial epicondyle.

Label Key
Mechanism
Repetitive wrist flexion + pronation loads the common flexor tendon.
Imaging
Change at the medial epicondyle common-tendon origin.
Clinical / real-world · why "golfer's" and why medial

The injured tendon is the common flexor origin from §7 — so the pain is medial (its mirror, "tennis elbow", hits the extensor origin on the lateral epicondyle). The provoking action is exactly what these muscles do: flex the wrist and pronate — the golf/throwing follow-through. And recall §1.1: the ulnar nerve lies just behind this same medial epicondyle, so symptoms can overlap with ulnar irritation. The anatomy names the sport.

R Recall checklist — L3
  • Distal humerus — capitulum (radius) + trochlea (ulna); radial & coronoid fossae (flexion, anterior) + olecranon fossa (extension, posterior); epicondyles (medial larger, ulnar nerve behind it).
  • Proximal radius/ulna — radius: head (on capitulum)/neck/radial tuberosity (biceps). Ulna: trochlear notch, coronoid, radial notch, olecranon (triceps), ulnar tuberosity (brachialis).
  • Elbow joint — synovial hinge (flexion/extension); capsule weak front/back, collaterals at sides (ulnar collateral = 3 bands); synovium continuous with proximal radioulnar joint; 3 bony points (triangle in flexion, line in extension); carrying angle (greater in females).
  • Radioulnar joints — both synovial pivots; anular ligament (proximal) + articular disc (distal, separates wrist joint); radius pivots over fixed ulna → pronation/supination; interosseous membrane binds + load-shares.
  • Elbow injuries — posterior dislocation (weak anterior capsule; ± collateral tear/fracture); pulled elbow (anular ligament); olecranon bursitis.
  • Arm muscles — anterior (musculocutaneous): biceps (flex + supinate, radial tuberosity), brachialis (chief flexor, ulna), coracobrachialis. Posterior (radial): triceps (chief extensor, olecranon; 3 heads) + anconeus.
  • Anterior forearm — common origin medial epicondyle; median except FCU + medial ½ FDP (ulnar). Superficial: PT, FCR, PL, FCU. Intermediate: FDS (middle phalanges, PIP). Deep: FPL, FDP (distal phalanges, DIP), pronator quadratus. Extrinsic = "remote control".
  • Golfer's elbow — medial epicondylitis; overuse of the flexor-pronator common tendon; wrist flexion + pronation sports; conservative treatment.
